newsitem.title: UK: UK's OFT seen about to rule on BA /American.
newsitem.headline: UK's OFT seen about to rule on BA /American.

text.p: Britain's Office of Fair Trading is expected to advise trade minister Ian Lang within the next few days whether or not British Airways' alliance with American Airlines should be referred to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.

Industry sources said interested government departments had discussed the findings of the OFT's three-month investigation into the alliance on Monday, clearing the way for the OFT to give Lang its advice within a matter of days.
But the sources said Lang is not expected to announce his verdict before the week after next.
Recent media and industry speculation has suggested that Lang will give the alliance qualified clearance, provided that BA's home hub of London Heathrow is opened up to competition.
BA and American's plans have attracted fierce criticism from rival airlines as well as consumer groups, who say the alliance will dominate the London trans-Atlantic market.

Under the alliance, BA intends to coordinate its 244 flights a week from Britain to 22 U.S. destinations with all of American's 238 flights a week from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.
They would also combine their frequent flyer programmes and share flight booking codes to promote their connecting flights on computer reservation systems.

BA and American argue their deal will lead to greater competition on British transatlantic routes because it will only go ahead if Britain and the U.S. liberalise the market with an "open skies" trade pact.

At the same time they say they must be allowed to combine to compete in the wider market against rival alliances such as that between United Airlines and Germany's Lufthansa for all-important transfer traffic.

"Open skies" talks between government negotiators broke down last month but there has been strong industry speculation that they will be reopened shortly with some concessions once the OFT verdict is known.

Industry sources say the main sticking points have been that American's U.S. rivals want their government to secure some of BA's 38 percent share of runway slots at London's Heathrow airport and also to be given "fifth freedom" rights to fly from Britain to third countries.

On the British side BA says it should not have to give up slots and arch rival Virgin Atlantic Airways says it wants British government negotiatiors to press for "cabotage" rights which would allow British airlines to fly domestic routes within the United States, and to be allowed to own U.S. airlines.
BA chief executive Robert Ayling said earlier this month that he expected "significant progress" on an open skies agreement by the end of September.
On the prospect of having to make concessions to get the alliance he said last week he was determined that the deal with American should be approved, "though not at any price."
